clue.text: A kiss in church for religious leader

indicators.note: 'in' places the first pair of words inside the word for a church

parts.note: CH is the standard abbreviation for church
taken as written
to lip is an old verb meaning to kiss

explanation.surface: A couple steal a kiss in church, in sight of the religious leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb sense of 'lip' as kissing is old-fashioned but in Chambers; the surface makes 'in church' look like a location rather than a container.
explanation.definitionFit: A caliph is the title of the chief Muslim ruler, successor to the Prophet as head of the faith.

clue.text: Sally's heavenly body almost touching rugby player

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a comet is a heavenly body
backs are the rugby players behind the scrum

explanation.surface: A woman named Sally, almost a goddess, is touching a rugby player.
explanation.walkthrough: Sally looks like a woman's name; it is a witty retort.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a quick witty remark, and a comeback is a sharp reply or retort.

clue.text: Left with drink, therefore this writer's feeling isolated

parts.note: L for left
as in 'just a quick one'
so means therefore
the setter refers to themself

explanation.surface: Abandoned with only a drink, the writer feels alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Lonesome means solitary and sad from lack of company, an adjective like the phrase.

clue.text: Having short bread?

parts.note: surface reading: owning shortbread, the Scottish butter biscuit
setter's reading: being short of money, bread being slang for cash

explanation.walkthrough: Shortbread is a crumbly Scottish biscuit; split it and 'bread' is slang for money, 'short' meaning lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lacking cash is hard up financially, without enough income to live comfortably.

clue.text: Whilst tight, laugh about hot pants

indicators.note: 'pants' is British slang for rubbish, so the preceding words are a mess to be put right

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone drunk laughs about a pair of hot pants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tight' (drunk) and 'about' only colour the surface; the letters come from 'laugh' and 'hot' alone. Pants, in British slang, means rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are conjunctions introducing a concession, as in 'whilst I agree, I still object'.

clue.text: Feel intense cold when out? Stay inside for a long time

definitions.text: Stay inside for a long time

indicators.note: 'out' can mean wrong or disordered, so the letters are put out of order

parts.note: taken as written
C for cold

explanation.surface: Advice about feeling the bitter cold outdoors: stay in for ages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' is slang for in prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A life sentence is a prison term for the rest of a convict's life, a very long stretch behind bars.

clue.text: Animal has almost contained hunger

indicators.note: contained means holding something inside, so one word goes within the other
almost means falling just short, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
a yen is a longing

explanation.surface: An animal has only just held its hunger in check.
explanation.walkthrough: HAS loses its S and then holds YEN.
explanation.definitionFit: The hyena is a carnivorous mammal of Africa and Asia, known for its laughing call.

clue.text: United Press ditch writer

parts.note: UP is the abbreviation for the news agency United Press
a dike is a ditch or trench

explanation.surface: A news agency drops one of its writers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ditch' looks like a verb meaning sack but is a noun. John Updike was the American novelist of the Rabbit books.
explanation.definitionFit: John Updike was a celebrated American novelist and short-story author, one example of a writer.

clue.text: Girl keeping identification card ultimately concealed

indicators.note: keeping means holding on to, so the girl wraps the next pieces

parts.note: hen is a colloquial term for a woman or girl
ID is short for identification

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of the word it follows

parts.note: the final letter of card

explanation.surface: A girl keeps her ID card well out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'identification card' looks like one item; split them.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean kept out of sight or secret, past participles describing something put away.

clue.text: Soldiers rejected rubbish advisor

parts.note: men are soldiers in the ranks

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the word for rubbish is read backwards

parts.note: rot is nonsense

explanation.surface: Troops have dismissed their counsellor's advice as rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: A mentor is a trusted counsellor who guides a less experienced person, named after Odysseus's friend.

clue.text: Rotten goal leads to Everton's dramatic upset

parts.note: food gone off is rotten
an end is an aim or goal

indicators.note: the leads of words are their front letters, which are the ones taken here

parts.note: the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A dreadful goal sparks a dramatic upset for Everton, the Liverpool football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goal' and 'upset' look like football; END is goal as an aim.
explanation.definitionFit: Upset in the sense of hurt or affronted by something said or done, an adjective matching the past participle.

clue.text: Prove aunt is best at rambling

indicators.note: rambling means wandering without order, so these letters stray into a new sequence

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Proof that an aunt is the best at rambling on.
explanation.definitionFit: To substantiate a claim is to provide evidence supporting it, establishing that it is true.

clue.text: Plant from stall is about to be returned

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the run of letters is read in the opposite direction
'from' says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

parts.note: the letters sitting across the end of the first word and the start of the last

explanation.surface: A garden-centre stall's plant is about to be sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like a reversal signal, but it is part of the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: Basil is an aromatic herb grown and used in cooking, especially in Italian dishes.

clue.text: Hairstyles with first cut and comb for free

indicators.note: having the first cut away means the opening letter is removed

parts.note: buns are hair gathered into a knot
a hackle is a steel comb for dressing flax

explanation.surface: Instructions for freeing hair: cut the buns first, then comb it loose.
explanation.walkthrough: BUNS loses its B. 'comb' looks like hairdressing but is the flax-dressing tool.
explanation.definitionFit: To free someone is to release them, exactly what removing shackles or fetters does.

clue.text: House seen renovated — good judgement

parts.note: the House of Commons, lower chamber of the UK Parliament

indicators.note: a renovated building has been remade, so these letters are rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Having the house seen and renovated shows good judgement.
explanation.definitionFit: Common sense is sound practical wisdom in everyday matters, the faculty of sensible decisions.

clue.text: Powerful canine welcomed by vet if fee's high

indicators.note: being welcomed means being taken inside, so one piece goes within the other
high means intoxicated, so these letters stagger out of order

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe-s
C stands for a canine tooth in dental notation

explanation.surface: A vet takes in a strong dog, provided the fee is high enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'canine' looks like a dog; in dentists' notation C marks a canine tooth.
explanation.definitionFit: Something effective produces the desired result, so a powerful remedy is an effective one.

clue.text: Pain in the head teacher's rear? Imagine rioting

indicators.note: rioting means running wild, so these letters break ranks
the rear of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the last letter of teacher
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rioting class gives the head teacher a pain in the backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head teacher' and 'pain in the rear' are both decoys; the definition is 'Pain in the head'.
explanation.definitionFit: A migraine is a severe recurring headache, often with nausea and disturbed vision.

clue.text: How's your father not with my wife?

definitions.text: How's your father not with my wife?

parts.note: surface reading: a question about the health of someone's dad

parts.words: How's your father not with my wife
parts.note: setter's reading: 'how's your father' is British slang for sex, here with someone other than one's own spouse

explanation.walkthrough: 'How's your father' is British euphemistic slang for sexual intercourse; having it with someone not your spouse is unfaithfulness.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the name for sexual relations between a married person and someone other than their spouse.

clue.text: Fan of dimmer switches to create mood

indicators.note: switches here means swaps around, so the letters change places

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who loves dimmer switches uses them to set a mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'switches' reads as the light switches themselves but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A frame of mind is a person's mental state or outlook at a given moment, much like a mood.

clue.text: A launch at sea

parts.note: taken as written
to float a company is to launch it on the stock market

explanation.surface: A boat is launched out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'launch' looks like a boat; it is the verb for starting a company.
explanation.definitionFit: Being at sea means being on the water rather than ashore, which is to be buoyant on the waves.

clue.text: Funny upper-class name? Considerably

parts.note: U is the old label for upper-class usage
N for name
as in 'well over budget'

explanation.surface: Someone's posh name is considerably amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny' looks like comical, but here it means feeling slightly ill.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling funny means feeling slightly ill or off-colour, in poor health.

clue.text: Wonderful soft drink — it's flipping cold

parts.note: Fanta is a brand of fizzy orange drink

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the short word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
C for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A grumble: the fizzy drink is great, but it's flipping cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' looks like a mild British swear word for emphasis, but it reverses the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Fantastic is used informally as praise for something extraordinarily good or marvellous.

clue.text: White bird follows a second

parts.note: taken as written
S for second
a hen is a female bird

explanation.surface: A white bird trails another by a second.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashen describes a face gone pale or grey from shock or illness, the colour of ash.

clue.text: Conservative with a capacity to ignore conclusion? Thatcher, perhaps

indicators.note: ignoring the conclusion means leaving off the final letter

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
taken as written
a role is a capacity or function, as in 'in her capacity as chair'

explanation.surface: A Conservative in some capacity, ignoring the conclusion: surely Margaret Thatcher.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at Margaret Thatcher, but the definition is her daughter Carol Thatcher, the journalist. ROLE loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Carol is a first name, and Carol Thatcher, the broadcaster daughter of the former Prime Minister, is one example.

clue.text: Above average

definitions.meaning: first meaning: up in the air, over one's head
second meaning: an old adjective sense, general or taken as an average across the whole

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as the phrase 'above average'; split it into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adverb or adjective for something positioned up high, and Chambers also gives it the rarer adjective sense of general or averaged.

clue.text: Characters in Australia I seldom get in touch with

indicators.note: the letters wanted are characters sitting inside the following words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the lone letter and the start of the last

explanation.surface: Someone who seldom contacts anybody in Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: To liaise is to establish contact and cooperation, communicating with another person or group.

clue.text: Story about hospital department? Daughter's gifted

indicators.note: 'about' means going around, so the story's word wraps the department

parts.note: a tale is a story
ENT is ear, nose and throat
D for daughter, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A story about a hospital ward reveals that someone's daughter is brilliant.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe a person with natural ability or a special aptitude for something.

clue.text: Just two lakes, yes?

parts.note: a mere is a lake, and L abbreviates lake
Y is short for yes

explanation.surface: A query about whether there are really only two lakes.
explanation.definitionFit: As adverbs both mean only or simply, as in 'it was just a scratch'.
